events.text: A fever comes in the night and does not go. In it you hear bells, seven of them, a long way off, and an old woman singing in a language you almost know. In the morning there is a bell-shaped bruise on your palm.

You wait. The fever waits too. It is better at it than you.
You climb to the Shrine of Seven Bells on the third day of the fever and ask for the rite.

events.text: Spirit-Mother Bongnye shakes seven bells over your head in the shrine yard. On the fifth one she stops, puts her hand on your forehead, and sighs. "You will be sick now," she says, "until you answer them. I am sorry. I was too."

effects.log: "Only to be heard," she says. "That is all the dead ever want. It is a great deal."
She nods, as if she knew you would.

effects.log: She gives you a straw charm for the fever. It helps a little.

events.text: The fever comes, and with it a dead grandmother you never met, sitting at the end of your bed and knitting. She looks up and says your name. The bells start somewhere behind her.

effects.log: She smiles and goes on knitting. In the morning there is a ball of grey wool on your pillow.

events.text: The sickness of the calling has a shape now. You cannot keep food down on the days of the dead, and on the first and fifteenth of every month you hear the bells. Spirit-Mother Bongnye sends a boy down with a message: the door is open.

effects.log: You go up. The boy carries your bag and does not look at your hands.

events.text: A physician from the town looks at your tongue and your eyes and your pulse and goes white. "There is nothing wrong with you," he says, "that medicine can reach." He does not charge you.

effects.log: You laugh. He does not.

events.text: The initiation gut lasts three days. On the third, Spirit-Mother Bongnye has you climb barefoot onto two straw-cutter blades set edge up. You stand on them and do not bleed. The village goes quiet. Then the spirits come down into you and speak through your mouth, and you do not remember what they say.

effects.log: "Your grandmother's name," Bongnye says, "and a debt in the next valley. We will go next spring."

effects.log: You sleep. When you wake the fever is gone and the bells are quiet, waiting.

events.text: Mudang Seori, Bongnye's other student, ties the five-coloured robe on you after the rite. She is younger than you and has been a mudang since she was nine. "The first wonhon is the hardest," she says. "After that, they are all the first."

effects.log: Hers was a drowned boy. She sang him home on her tenth birthday and cried for a week.

effects.log: "Do not thank me," she says. "They will ask again. Maybe not in this life."
